leads.title: Polyethylene at ICI in Cheshire
leads.why: Found by accident under very high pressure, polyethylene insulated wartime radar cables and became the most produced plastic in the world, the stuff of films, bags, bottles and pipes.
leads.verify: Confirm the 1933 observation by Fawcett and Gibson, the reproducible synthesis of 1935 and the start of production in 1939. Note the low-pressure catalytic routes of 1953 (Ziegler at Mulheim, Hogan and Banks at Phillips), which connect to the dataset's polypropylene record and may need their own.

leads.title: Barkcloth (tapa) in the Pacific Islands
leads.where: Island Southeast Asia, Near Oceania and Polynesia
leads.date: carried into Remote Oceania from c. 1300 to 800 BCE
leads.why: Austronesian voyagers carried the paper mulberry and the beater across the Pacific, where barkcloth replaced the loom as the source of clothing, bedding, sails' lashings, gifts and sacred wrappings.
leads.verify: Trace the evidence for the origin of beaten barkcloth in southern China and Southeast Asia (stone beaters from the Pearl River region, perhaps 6000 BCE or earlier, which should be the first-known record) and the genetic and archaeological evidence for paper mulberry moving with Lapita and Polynesian settlers. Barkcloth in Central Africa and bark-beating in Mesoamerica appear to be independent.

leads.title: Engineered paved road network of Rome
leads.why: Surveyed, drained, hard-surfaced roads tied together the Mediterranean world and set many of Europe's later routes.
leads.verify: The Via Appia (312 BCE) as the start of systematic building, construction methods as excavated (not only as Vitruvius or later writers imply), and the size of the network at its peak. Check what Rome owed to Etruscan roads and to the Persian royal roads; the Persian system and the Qin and Han imperial highways each merit a record under this concept.

leads.title: Iron-chain suspension bridges in southwest China and the Himalaya
leads.date: rope bridges by the 1st century BCE; iron chains by c. 600 CE (earlier claims contested)
leads.why: Chain bridges opened mountain trade routes, and European accounts of them from the seventeenth century fed the first Western designs.
leads.verify: The earliest reliable date for iron-chain bridges (claims range from the first to the seventh century CE), the older bamboo- and rope-cable bridges behind them, and Thangtong Gyalpo's fifteenth-century Tibetan bridges. Establish what the builders of the first Western suspension bridges (Finley, 1801) knew of them.

leads.title: Controlled-access motorways in Italy and Germany
leads.where: Lombardy, Italy; Berlin and the Rhineland, Germany
leads.why: National motorway networks reshaped freight, travel and the form of cities in most countries during the twentieth century.
leads.verify: The dated firsts and what each was: the AVUS in Berlin (1921), the Milan to the lakes autostrada (1924), the Cologne to Bonn road (1932), and the Long Island Motor Parkway (1908) and American parkways as precedents. The hard surfaces behind them (macadam, c. 1816; asphalt and concrete paving) may merit a record of their own.

leads.title: Organised night-soil collection in the cities of Song China
leads.where: Hangzhou and the lower Yangtze, China
leads.why: Selling waste instead of dumping it kept very large cities comparatively clean and returned nutrients to intensively farmed land, a system that lasted in East Asia into the twentieth century.
leads.verify: The earliest documents for paid collectors and a market in night soil (Chen Fu's farming treatise of 1149; descriptions of Hangzhou in the thirteenth century), how far back the practice goes, and the later commercial trade in Edo Japan, which may merit a derived record.
